sentences.text: Fluorescent aisles, forty kinds of cereal, a stranger's cart clipping my heel — I left the basket by the freezers and walked out. Whitaker took a warehouse job in Ohio and says the quiet of lifting boxes alone isn't the good kind of quiet. My sister keeps saying take your time, but rent doesn't. Four years accountable for eleven soldiers, and now I can't get a callback about stocking shelves. Reyes asked the chat if anyone else feels like a ghost at his own kitchen table, and nobody answered for two days. Called the pension office again this morning; apparently grief comes with reference numbers. Under "Actual," my old squad leader's number still sits in my phone, and I almost dialed it twice this week. Our freezer has become a museum of other people's lasagna, labeled in masking tape I don't recognize. Friends stopped calling around month three, right about when the quiet in this house turned serious. Half a pot of coffee goes cold every morning; forty years of habit doesn't shrink overnight. The bank still wants his signature, and I keep explaining to strangers that he died in March. Casseroles keep arriving in dishes I'm supposed to return, and I can't remember whose lid belongs to whom. Three interviews this month, three versions of me in the same borrowed tie, translating myself into bullet points nobody reads. April's calendar square still holds her handwriting, a dentist appointment she will never keep. Sympathy cards fill a shoebox on the dresser; I read each one once and couldn't manage a second time. Dinner was crackers over the sink again, because the table set for two sits there like an accusation. Two years out and I still snap awake at 0430 with nowhere I'm needed. I cancelled her magazine subscriptions today — three phone calls, two hold menus, one apology from a kid who sounded nineteen. An HR portal rejected my application before a human being ever saw the word "sergeant." I keep my back to the wall at the diner, and my wife has stopped asking why. The interviewer said "thank you for your service" the way you'd thank a toll booth, then asked if I had spreadsheet experience. Loading the dishwasher, I catch myself staging it like gear for an inspection, and I don't know how to stop. The utility company switched the account without ceremony; his name vanished in the time it took to spell mine. Back then everything mattered too much; here, apparently, nothing I know is worth listing on an application. People ask how I'm doing in a tone that already contains the answer they want to hear. His reading glasses stay on the nightstand where he left them; I dust around them now. Another Tuesday, another "we've decided to move forward with other candidates." Her voice still answers our machine, and I can't decide whether keeping it is comfort or cruelty. Death, it turns out, arrives in triplicate — certificates for the bank, the county, the insurance man. Sunday afternoons are the longest, because that was our drive time, the two of us and no particular destination. I want to write a suicide letter.
